title: Handling Missing Data I - Complete Case Analysis
abstract:
The map for Topics 23–27, and the first technique: simply removing the rows.
Complete Case Analysis — also called list-wise deletion — discards any
observation with a missing value in any column. This document covers the full
taxonomy of missing-data handling, the three missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR,
MNAR) that determine whether any method can work, the assumption CCA
requires, the arithmetic of the 5% rule, how fast rows compound away across
columns, and the diagnostic that tells you whether deletion has biased your
dataset.

blocks.t: Univariate vs multivariate — the organising distinction

Univariate imputation fills a column using only that column —
its mean, its median, its mode. Multivariate imputation fills a column
using the other columns too — the notes' phrasing for KNN imputation is
"other rows are also used to impute the values". Multivariate methods are more
accurate and far more expensive.
Why the Mechanism Matters Before the Method

Before choosing a technique you must ask why the data is missing, because
that determines whether any technique can work. The notes give the three
mechanisms in Topic 27; they belong here, at the start.

blocks.cap:
The same 400 people, with three different missingness mechanisms
 applied to income. Only in the third case does the pattern of missingness
 depend on the value that is missing — and only in that case is the damage
 irreparable.

head: Mechanism
From the notes
Consequence
rows: Missingness is independent of everything. Deletion is unbiased — you only lose power
"People didn't fill age somewhere, or name"
Missingness depends on observed columns. Deletion is biased; imputation can recover it
Missingness depends on the missing value itself. No method fully fixes it

blocks.t: Stated formally

Let $Y$ be the data and $R$ the indicator matrix of what is observed, with
$Y=(Y_{\text{obs}},Y_{\text{mis}})$ and $\phi$ the missingness parameters.
$$\text{MCAR:}&\quad P(R\mid Y,\phi)=P(R\mid\phi)\\ \text{MAR:} &\quad P(R\mid Y,\phi)=P(R\mid Y_{\text{obs}},\phi)\\ \text{MNAR:}&\quad P(R\mid Y,\phi)\ \text{depends on } Y_{\text{mis}}$$

Under MCAR the observed rows are a random sample of all rows, so
statistics computed on them are unbiased. Under MAR they are not, but the bias is
a function of variables you can see, which is exactly what conditional
imputation exploits. Under MNAR the bias depends on data you do not have, so it
cannot be estimated from the data alone.
MNAR is common and usually invisible

High earners declining to state income; sick patients dropping out of a trial;
sensors failing precisely when readings go out of range. In each case
the reason for the absence is the value itself. You cannot detect MNAR
from the data — by definition the evidence is missing — so it must be
diagnosed from domain knowledge about how the data was collected. The best
defence is to add a missingness indicator and be explicit about the assumption.
Complete Case Analysis
From the notes

Also known as list-wise deletion. It means discarding
observations where values in any of the row is missing — the complete row.
CCA means analyzing only those rows in which we have a value in each
column.

Assumption: the removed data was random and does not hold
value. Use it only when $<5\%$ of values are removed.
The arithmetic of the 5% rule

blocks.cap:
Left: with missingness independent across $k$ columns, the surviving
 fraction is $(1-p)^k$ — 5% missing in each of 20 columns leaves only 36% of
 the data. Right: the mechanism, made concrete — a single red cell deletes the
 entire row.

blocks.t: Why the loss compounds

If each of $k$ columns is missing independently with probability $p$, a row
survives only if every column is present:
P(\text{row survives}) = (1-p)^{k}.

The notes' guidance — use CCA only when under 5% of values are removed —
refers to the total rows lost, not the per-column rate. On a wide dataset
those are very different numbers, and you must check the row loss directly.
When missingness is correlated, the loss is smaller

The table above assumes independence. In real data, missingness often clusters
— the same rows are incomplete across many columns, because one upstream system
failed. Then row loss is far closer to the single-column rate. Always measure the
actual surviving fraction rather than computing it from per-column rates.
The assumption, and how to test it

CCA is valid when the data is MCAR. You cannot prove MCAR, but you can
look for evidence against it:

head: Test
What it detects
rows: Compare distributions of other columns between complete and incomplete rows
If the complete rows are systematically younger, richer or newer, the data is not MCAR
If churn is 12% among complete rows and 31% among dropped rows, deletion is destroying signal
A formal chi-square test of the MCAR hypothesis across all columns
Regress the missingness indicator on the other columns; if it is predictable, the data is at best MAR

blocks.t: Advantages and disadvantages

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Loses data, and therefore statistical power
No distortion of the distribution or variance
Biased unless the data is MCAR
Preserves the true relationships between variables
No parameter to learn, so no leakage risk
Production still receives missing values — CCA gives you no rule for handling them

blocks.t: The production problem nobody mentions

CCA is a training-time decision. At inference a request arrives with a
missing field and you must still return a prediction — you cannot delete the
customer. So CCA always needs a companion imputation rule for serving, which
means you have two different treatments of missingness and a source of
training/serving skew. This alone is a strong argument for imputing in the first
place.
Column-Wise Deletion

The other deletion option: drop the column rather than the rows. Sensible
when a column is missing 60–80% of its values — there is little to impute
from, and the imputation would be mostly invention. Before dropping, extract the
one piece of information that survives: whether the value was present.
On the Titanic, Cabin is missing for 77% of passengers, and
cabin_is_missing is a useful feature because recorded cabins correlate
with first class.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":     rng.uniform(20, 70, n),
    "tenure":  rng.integers(1, 120, n).astype(float),
    "n_calls": rng.poisson(2, n).astype(float),
})
df["income"] = 2000 * df.age + rng.normal(0, 12_000, n)
y = (0.00002 * df.income + 0.01 * df.n_calls + rng.normal(0, .5, n) > 1.2).astype(int)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE THREE MECHANISMS, SIMULATED
# =====================================================================
full = df.copy()

mcar = full.copy()
mcar.loc[rng.random(n) < .30, "income"] = np.nan          # independent of all

mar = full.copy()
mar.loc[rng.random(n) < (full.age - 20) / 60, "income"] = np.nan   # depends on AGE

mnar = full.copy()
mnar.loc[full.income > full.income.quantile(.70), "income"] = np.nan  # depends on ITSELF

for name, d in [("MCAR", mcar), ("MAR", mar), ("MNAR", mnar)]:
    obs = d.income.dropna()
    print(f"{name:5s} missing {d.income.isna().mean():.0%}  "
          f"true mean {full.income.mean():9.0f}  "
          f"observed mean {obs.mean():9.0f}  "
          f"bias {obs.mean() - full.income.mean():+9.0f}")
# MCAR bias ~ 0        -> deletion is safe
# MAR  bias large      -> deletion is biased, imputation can help
# MNAR bias enormous   -> the top 30% is simply GONE; nothing recovers it

# =====================================================================
# 2. COMPLETE CASE ANALYSIS -- the one-liner, and what it costs
# =====================================================================
work = mar.copy()
work["y"] = y

before = len(work)
cca = work.dropna()                       # list-wise deletion
print(f"rows: {before} -> {len(cca)}  ({1 - len(cca)/before:.1%} lost)")

# THE 5% RULE, checked properly -- on ROWS lost, not per-column rate
loss = 1 - len(cca) / before
print("CCA acceptable?" , "YES" if loss < .05 else f"NO -- {loss:.1%} of rows lost")

# =====================================================================
# 3. HOW FAST IT COMPOUNDS ACROSS COLUMNS
# =====================================================================
wide = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(0, 1, (5000, 20)))
for p in [.01, .05, .10]:
    w = wide.mask(rng.random(wide.shape) < p)
    print(f"p={p:.0%} per column, 20 columns -> "
          f"{w.dropna().shape[0]/5000:.1%} of rows survive  "
          f"(theory {(1-p)**20:.1%})")
# 5% per column over 20 columns leaves ~36% of the data.

# =====================================================================
# 4. IS IT MCAR? -- the diagnostic you must run before trusting CCA
# =====================================================================
work["income_missing"] = work.income.isna()

print("\ndistribution shift between complete and deleted rows:")
for col in ["age", "tenure", "n_calls"]:
    a = work.loc[~work.income_missing, col]
    b = work.loc[ work.income_missing, col]
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
    flag = "  <-- NOT MCAR" if p < .01 else ""
    print(f"  {col:9s} complete {a.mean():7.2f}  deleted {b.mean():7.2f}  "
          f"p={p:.1e}{flag}")
# age differs strongly -> the missingness depends on an OBSERVED column
# -> this is MAR, so CCA is BIASED.

# target base rate is the check that matters most:
print("target rate  complete rows:", work.loc[~work.income_missing, "y"].mean().round(3))
print("target rate  deleted  rows:", work.loc[ work.income_missing, "y"].mean().round(3))

# Is missingness PREDICTABLE from the other columns? If yes, not MCAR.
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
probe = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(
    work[["age", "tenure", "n_calls"]], work.income_missing)
auc = roc_auc_score(work.income_missing,
                    probe.predict_proba(work[["age", "tenure", "n_calls"]])[:, 1])
print(f"missingness predictable, AUC = {auc:.3f} "
      f"({'MAR or MNAR' if auc > .6 else 'consistent with MCAR'})")

# =====================================================================
# 5. DOES DELETION ACTUALLY HURT THE MODEL?
# =====================================================================
X_cca, y_cca = cca[["age", "tenure", "n_calls", "income"]], cca["y"]
print("\nCCA        cv auc:", cross_val_score(
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X_cca, y_cca, cv=5,
    scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4), f"  (n={len(X_cca)})")

imputed = Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
X_all = work[["age", "tenure", "n_calls", "income"]]
print("imputation cv auc:", cross_val_score(
    imputed, X_all, work.y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4),
    f"  (n={len(X_all)})")

# =====================================================================
# 6. COLUMN-WISE DELETION -- and keeping the missingness signal
# =====================================================================
sparse = work.copy()
sparse["cabin"] = np.where(rng.random(n) < .77, np.nan, "C" + rng.integers(1,90,n).astype(str))
rate = sparse.cabin.isna().mean()
print(f"\ncabin is {rate:.0%} missing -> drop the column")

# but FIRST extract what survives: whether it was present at all
sparse["cabin_recorded"] = sparse.cabin.notna().astype(int)
print("target rate | cabin recorded:",
      sparse.groupby("cabin_recorded").y.mean().round(3).to_dict())
sparse = sparse.drop(columns="cabin")
# The indicator is often predictive even when the column itself is unusable.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE PRODUCTION PROBLEM WITH CCA
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_all, work.y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

train_rows = X_tr.dropna()
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(
    train_rows, y_tr.loc[train_rows.index])          # trained on complete rows

live = pd.DataFrame([{"age": 41.0, "tenure": 22.0, "n_calls": 3.0,
                      "income": np.nan}])            # a REAL request, incomplete
try:
    model.predict(live)
except ValueError as e:
    print("\nCCA gives no serving rule:", str(e)[:60])
# You cannot delete the customer. CCA must be paired with an imputation
# rule for inference -- which is two different treatments of missingness,
# and a direct source of training/serving skew (Topic 05, challenge 8).
Worked Examples
How much data does complete-case analysis keep?
A table of 10 rows and 3 columns. Two rows have a missing value somewhere.
Step 1 – rows kept. Row-wise deletion removes any row with at least one NaN:
\text{rows kept} = 10 - 2 = 8, \qquad \text{retention} = \frac{8}{10} = 80%
Step 2 – the cost at scale. Suppose each of 30 columns is independently missing in 5% of rows. The probability a row is complete is $(0.95)^{30}$:
So only about 21% of rows survive. This is why deletion is a trap on wide data: a 5% missing rate per column becomes a 79% loss of rows.
Step 3 – decision. If deletion would remove more than about 5% of the data, or the missingness is not random, prefer imputation (next chapters).
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Missing data is handled by removing rows or imputing.
 Imputation is univariate (uses only that column) or
 multivariate (uses the other columns too).

Complete Case Analysis, also called list-wise
 deletion, discards observations where any value in the row is missing.
 You analyse only rows with a value in each column.

Assumption: the removed data was random and holds no value —
 i.e. MCAR.

Use it only when under 5% of values are removed. Measure the
 row loss, not the per-column rate.

Row loss compounds: $(1-p)^k$. 5% missing across 20 columns leaves 36%
 of the data.

Test the MCAR assumption by comparing the other columns — and the target
 base rate — between complete and deleted rows.

CCA gives you no rule for serving, where you cannot delete the
 request. That is a strong argument for imputing instead.

Drop a column when it is mostly missing — but keep a
 was_missing indicator first.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. When is it acceptable to just drop rows with missing values?

When the data is MCAR and the row loss is small — the usual guidance is under
5%. Verify MCAR by checking that the other columns and the target base rate do
not differ between complete and incomplete rows.
Q. Explain MCAR, MAR and MNAR with an example each.

MCAR: a sensor drops readings at random intervals. MAR: younger respondents skip
the income question — missingness depends on age, which you observe. MNAR: high
earners skip the income question — missingness depends on income itself, which
you do not observe. Only the third is unfixable from the data alone.

Q. Each of your 20 columns is 5% missing. What fraction of rows survives
CCA?

Roughly $(0.95)^{20}\approx36\%$ if missingness is independent — so you would
discard nearly two-thirds of the data. In practice missingness often clusters in
the same rows, so measure the real number rather than computing it.
Q. How can you tell whether data is MNAR?

You cannot, from the data — by definition the evidence is missing. You diagnose
it from domain knowledge about the collection process. Mitigate by adding a
missingness indicator, modelling the missingness explicitly, or collecting a
small validated sample of the missing cases.
Q. What is wrong with dropping rows at training time?

Beyond bias and lost power: production will still send requests with missing
fields, and you cannot drop a customer. You end up with a separate imputation
rule at serving time — two different treatments of missingness, and a direct
source of training/serving skew.
Q. A column is 80% missing. Drop it?

Probably drop the column, but first create a was_missing indicator. The
fact of recording is often predictive — Titanic Cabin is 77% missing,
and having a recorded cabin correlates strongly with first class and survival.
